vignette:
He doesn’t talk about it in the first session. He sits forward on the edge of the armchair, hands resting on his knees, dressed in his blue transit-issue polo shirt even though it’s his day off. He tells me he’s a bus driver, has been for almost twenty years. He likes the route—the same one for the last twelve—because he knows every pothole, every stoplight, every regular who boards with a nod or a monthly pass. He says he still likes the work, but lately it’s been harder to get out of bed.

By the third session, he tells me about the night that changed everything. It was a little over a year ago, just after eleven p.m., on the last run of his shift. He was heading back to the depot along a stretch of road that cuts through an industrial park. He saw a patrol car pulled over at an awkward angle, lights off, door ajar. He slowed. Two officers were struggling with a man on the ground, shouting. He remembers hearing a pop—not loud, more like a branch snapping—and then one of the officers stepped back, looked at his hands. The man on the ground stopped moving.

He pulled over. He didn’t call it in; he just sat in the driver’s seat, engine idling, watching. One officer walked toward the bus, flashlight raised, and told him to move along. He drove away. He never gave a statement. He never even told his supervisor.

He says he didn’t feel anything at first. He finished his shift, went home, ate a sandwich, watched a little TV. But over the next weeks, he started to feel a tightness in his chest whenever he passed that intersection. He started taking a different route to the depot, adding ten minutes to his commute. Then he began to avoid driving at night altogether, swapping shifts with a coworker who needed overtime. He told himself it was just fatigue.

Now, in session, he describes the dreams. Not every night, but three or four times a week. He’s back in the driver’s seat, but the bus is moving on its own, speeding toward the scene, and he can’t stop it. He wakes up drenched in sweat, heart pounding, convinced he hears that pop. He checks the locks on his apartment door twice before he can go back to sleep.

On his route, he has become hypervigilant. He scans every parked car, every shadow near a bus stop. He flinches when a police cruiser passes—not with anger, he says, but with a cold dread that makes his hands tremble on the wheel. He once pulled over because he thought he saw a body lying on the sidewalk; it was a discarded jacket. A passenger asked if he was okay, and he snapped at her, something he’d never done before. He apologized later, but the shame stayed with him all week.

He has started to withdraw. He used to have coffee after a shift with a few other drivers, but now he drives straight home and doesn’t answer his phone. He hasn’t been on a date in months. He says the world feels different, like there’s a film of grime over everything he sees. He feels detached from his passengers, from the chatter on the radio, from the ordinary rhythm of the city he once found comforting.

Last week, he almost quit. He was stopped at a red light when a police SUV pulled up alongside him. The officer inside looked over, and for a second he thought the officer was staring right at him, like he knew. His heart started racing, his vision tunneled, and he felt like he was going to pass out. He managed to pull into a gas station and sat in the lot for twenty minutes, gripping the steering wheel, telling himself it was just a normal traffic stop.

He doesn’t know why it happened to him. He wasn’t the one being arrested. He wasn’t the one who fired the shot. He was just a guy driving a bus, going home. But he can’t shake the feeling that he should have done something, called for help, done anything other than drive away. That guilt sits on his chest like a second passenger.
